remotecmd-cli: Run shell commands, copy files and forward ports on remote machines through a WebSocket relay: no SSH keys, no inbound ports, no VPN.
one_liner: Each remote machine runs a daemon that dials OUT to a relay; you run the CLI, which also connects to the relay and asks it to forward a command to a named target. The target's token, which you hold, is the only thing that authorises the command.

model.topology: you (CLI) --ws--> relay <--ws-- target daemon. Every connection is outbound; the relay is the only listener.
model.relay: A hub (relay daemon start) that routes messages between CLIs and daemons by target name. It does not run commands. Self-host it anywhere public; it listens on all interfaces, port 3032 by default.
model.daemon: Runs on each target (daemon start). Registers under a name with its token and executes whatever the relay forwards with that token, as the user it runs as.
model.client: The CLI on your machine. Holds one token per target in config.json and sends execute requests; it never accepts commands itself.
model.direction: Control is one-way. Adding a target does not expose your machine: its daemon's token comes to you, never the reverse. A machine is only controllable if it runs a daemon.
model.config: ~/.remotecmd/config.json (relay URL, this node's name, optional relay secret, targets and groups). RCMD_CONFIG_DIR points one process at another directory, which is how one machine talks to a second relay or runs a second daemon.
model.names: A name is unique per relay. A name held by a live connection can only be re-registered with the same token, so nobody can take over a connected node's name.

loop: On the relay host: remotecmd-cli relay daemon start --port 3032 -daemon (set RELAY_SECRET to require a shared secret).
On your machine: remotecmd-cli set-relay --url http://<relay>:3032 --name <you>.
Add a target, either by pairing (remotecmd-cli pair listen, then run the printed one-liner on the target) or manually (daemon start on the target, then add-target --name <n> --token <its token>).
Run commands: remotecmd-cli exec --target <n> --cmd 'hostname'. Use --targets or --group for many at once, and --format json to parse the result.
Move data or reach services: cp for files, tunnel start for ports.
Keep nodes alive across reboots: remotecmd-cli daemon systemd install (schtasks on Windows).

concepts.target: A named remote machine running a daemon. Your config maps the name to its token and, if the daemon registered under a different name, to relay_name.
concepts.token: The per-daemon secret. The daemon registers with it and every command must carry it. Keep it like an SSH private key: whoever holds it can run commands as the daemon's user.
concepts.relay secret: An optional shared secret (RELAY_SECRET on the relay, set-relay --secret on clients) that gates who may connect to the relay at all. It is separate from target tokens.
concepts.group: A named list of targets for multi-target exec (group create/add/remove/delete/list).
concepts.pairing: pair listen prints a one-liner and a short code; the joining daemon sends its token to the listener, which saves it as a target. --require-activation-key stops anyone else who sees the code from pairing.
concepts.stream: --stream sends stdout/stderr as they are produced instead of one buffered result. Use it for long commands.
concepts.health: list-targets probes targets unseen for over an hour; --refresh probes all of them now. Results are cached in health.json.

execute: remotecmd-cli client   (one JSON command per line on stdin)
daemon (on targets): remotecmd-cli daemon update [--check] [--force]   (updates the binary the running daemon uses, then restarts it in place)
remotecmd-cli daemon systemd install|remove   (schtasks on Windows)
relay (on the hub): remotecmd-cli relay daemon stop | relay daemon status [--json]   (health: GET /_health)

examples.goal: Check disk space on one machine
Run the same command on a fleet and parse the results
Reach a database that only listens on the target's loopback
Onboard a new machine without copying tokens by hand
Talk to a second relay without touching the main config

gotchas: A target token is equivalent to shell access as the daemon's user (often root). Never paste it into logs, tickets or chat.
Only machines that run a daemon can be controlled. The client side never accepts commands, and tunnel ports bind 127.0.0.1 only.
The relay operator sees every token and command. TLS (--tls-cert/--tls-key or a TLS proxy) protects the wire, not the relay itself. Run your own relay for anything sensitive.
Set RELAY_SECRET on any public relay; without it anyone can connect and register names. RELAY_SECRET_EXEMPT lets listed names skip the secret.

RCMD_CONFIG_DIR only exists in recent builds. An older binary silently ignores it and writes ~/.remotecmd/config.json instead. Before running set-relay or add-target against an alternate directory, check that remotecmd-cli help-json lists RCMD_CONFIG_DIR under env. If help-json doesn't exist, the binary is too old.
Old daemons lack newer protocol features (for example stdin passthrough). A newer client then fails or hangs against them; upgrade the daemon.

Exit codes are legacy: 1 = remote command failed, 2 = relay unreachable (retry), 3 = bad arguments or config, 4 = internal. Errors are JSON on stderr when stderr is not a terminal (RCMD_ERROR_FORMAT=json|text to force).
A daemon reconnects every 5s; a dead link is noticed within about 60s by both ends via WebSocket pings, and dials give up after 10s.

Two daemons on one machine: to join a second relay give it its own RCMD_CONFIG_DIR; to run under a second name on the same relay use daemon start --name <n>. With -daemon, pass the same --name to daemon stop/status, since each name gets its own PID file.
update verifies the release's sha256 and refuses to install on any doubt (exit 100).

update replaces the CLI you invoked; daemon update / relay daemon update replace the binary the running daemon or relay actually executes (it may be a different file) and restart it in place — fleet-wide: rcx --group <g> 'remotecmd-cli daemon update'.
